diagnostic.question: What is the primary advantage of a DBMS over a traditional file-processing system?
diagnostic.optionA: Centralized control of data with reduced redundancy and inconsistency
diagnostic.optionC: It eliminates the need for a query language

diagnostic.question: In the ER model, an "entity" is best described as:
diagnostic.optionB: A real-world object or concept that can be distinctly identified

diagnostic.question: In the relational model, a "relation" corresponds to what everyday database concept?
diagnostic.optionB: A table consisting of rows and columns

diagnostic.question: Which SQL clause is used to filter rows BEFORE any grouping takes place?
Which relational algebra operator, symbolized by sigma (σ), selects rows (tuples) satisfying a given condition?
In the functional dependency notation X → Y, this means:
diagnostic.optionB: For any two tuples with the same value of X, their values of Y must also be the same
diagnostic.optionC: X and Y must always be equal
diagnostic.optionD: X is a foreign key to Y

diagnostic.question: A relation is in First Normal Form (1NF) if:
diagnostic.optionA: Every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key
diagnostic.optionB: All attribute values are atomic (indivisible), with no repeating groups or multivalued attributes
diagnostic.optionD: Every determinant is a candidate key

diagnostic.question: What does the "A" in ACID properties of a transaction stand for?
A "shared lock" (S-lock) on a data item allows:
diagnostic.optionA: Only the transaction holding it to read OR write the item
diagnostic.optionB: Multiple transactions to simultaneously hold a shared lock and read the item, but none may write it while any shared lock is held
diagnostic.optionC: Only one transaction to ever access the item again

diagnostic.question: What is the primary purpose of creating an index on a database column?
diagnostic.optionA: To enforce that the column cannot contain NULL values
diagnostic.optionB: To speed up data retrieval operations (searches) on that column, at some cost in storage and write overhead
diagnostic.optionC: To automatically encrypt the column's data
diagnostic.optionD: To reduce the number of columns in the table

practice.question: Which of the following is a typical service provided by a DBMS that a plain file system does NOT provide?

options.text: Storing bytes on disk
Enforcing data integrity constraints
Reading a file sequentially
Naming files

practice.explanation: A DBMS enforces integrity constraints (e.g., primary keys, foreign keys) declared in the schema; a raw file system has no concept of such constraints.

practice.question: In the three-schema architecture, which level describes how data is actually stored on disk?

options.text: External schema
Conceptual schema
Internal schema
View schema

practice.explanation: The internal (physical) schema specifies storage structures, file organization, and access paths used to store the data.

practice.question: "Logical data independence" is the capacity to change which schema without requiring changes to external schemas or application programs?

options.text: Internal schema only
Conceptual schema
Hardware configuration
Network protocol

practice.explanation: Logical data independence allows the conceptual schema to change (e.g., adding a new entity) without forcing changes to existing external views or the programs built on them.

practice.question: Which category of SQL statements is used to define or alter database structure, such as CREATE TABLE and DROP TABLE?

options.text: DML
DDL
DCL
TCL

practice.explanation: DDL (Data Definition Language) statements define and modify schema objects like tables, indexes, and views.

practice.question: Which SQL command category includes GRANT and REVOKE?

options.text: DDL
DML
DCL
TCL

practice.explanation: DCL (Data Control Language) statements such as GRANT and REVOKE manage user access permissions.

practice.question: In an ER diagram, a "relationship" represents:

options.text: An attribute value
An association among two or more entities
A primary key
A normalization rule

practice.explanation: A relationship captures how entities are associated with each other, such as a Student "enrolls in" a Course.

practice.question: A "weak entity" in the ER model is an entity type that:

options.text: Has no attributes at all
Does not have a key attribute of its own and depends on a related "owner" entity for identification
Can only exist in one database
Always has a 1:1 relationship

practice.explanation: A weak entity lacks sufficient attributes to form its own primary key and relies on its identifying (owner) entity, combined with a partial key, for unique identification.

practice.question: What distinguishes a "candidate key" from the chosen "primary key" of an entity?

options.text: A candidate key can have duplicate values while a primary key cannot
A candidate key is any attribute (or minimal set) that could uniquely identify instances; the primary key is the one candidate key selected to be the actual identifier
A primary key is always composite while a candidate key never is
There is no difference

practice.explanation: An entity may have multiple candidate keys (each capable of uniquely identifying instances); the database designer chooses one of them as the primary key.

practice.question: In ER modeling, "specialization" is the process of:

options.text: Merging two entity types into one
Defining subclasses of an entity type based on distinguishing characteristics
Removing all attributes from an entity
Converting an entity into a relationship

practice.explanation: Specialization takes a higher-level entity type (superclass) and defines one or more lower-level subclasses, each with attributes or relationships specific to that subclass (e.g., Employee specialized into Manager and Engineer).

practice.question: A "multivalued attribute" is one that:

options.text: Can hold more than one value for a single entity instance
Is always the primary key
Cannot appear in an ER diagram
Must be composite

practice.explanation: A multivalued attribute can take on multiple values simultaneously for a single entity instance, such as a Person having multiple PhoneNumbers.

practice.question: In ER specialization, "disjoint" constraint means:

options.text: An entity instance can belong to multiple subclasses simultaneously
An entity instance can belong to at most one subclass of the specialization
All entity instances must belong to a subclass
No entity instance can belong to any subclass

practice.explanation: A disjoint constraint means each entity instance of the superclass can be a member of at most one of the specialization subclasses at a time, as opposed to "overlapping" where it could belong to multiple.

practice.question: In relational model terminology, a "tuple" corresponds to a:

options.text: Column of a table
Row of a table
Table name
Database name

practice.explanation: A tuple is a single, ordered set of attribute values - exactly one row of a relation.

practice.question: What is a "foreign key"?

options.text: An attribute that must always be unique within its own table
An attribute (or set of attributes) in one relation that references the primary key of another (or the same) relation
A key used only for encryption
A synonym for primary key

practice.explanation: A foreign key establishes a link between two relations by referencing the primary key values of another relation, enforcing referential integrity.

practice.question: The "entity integrity" constraint states that:

options.text: Foreign key values must always exist in the referenced relation
No primary key attribute of a base relation may contain a NULL value
All attributes must be numeric
Every relation must have exactly five attributes

practice.explanation: Entity integrity requires that the primary key, which uniquely identifies tuples, can never be NULL, since a NULL value could not meaningfully identify a tuple.

practice.question: The "referential integrity" constraint requires that:

options.text: Every attribute value must be unique across the whole table
A foreign key value must either match an existing primary key value in the referenced relation or be NULL
Tables must not have more than 10 attributes
Primary keys must always be numeric

practice.explanation: Referential integrity ensures that any non-NULL foreign key value in the referencing relation must correspond to an existing primary key value in the referenced relation, preventing "dangling" references.

practice.question: What is a "super key"?

options.text: A key that can never uniquely identify tuples
Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples in a relation, which may include additional, unnecessary attributes beyond a minimal candidate key
A synonym for foreign key
A key that only exists in weak entities

practice.explanation: A super key is any attribute set that uniquely identifies tuples; a candidate key is defined as a minimal super key.

practice.question: An INNER JOIN between two tables returns:

options.text: All rows from both tables regardless of match
Only rows that have matching values in both tables based on the join condition
Only rows from the left table
Only rows from the right table

practice.explanation: INNER JOIN returns only the rows where the join condition is satisfied in both tables, excluding unmatched rows from either side.

practice.question: Which SQL aggregate function returns the number of rows in a result set?

options.text: SUM()
COUNT()
AVG()
MAX()

practice.explanation: COUNT() returns the number of rows (or non-NULL values of a specified column) matching the query.

practice.question: Which clause is used to filter groups AFTER GROUP BY has been applied, typically based on an aggregate condition?

options.text: WHERE
HAVING
ON
LIMIT

practice.explanation: HAVING filters aggregated groups (e.g., only departments with COUNT(*) > 5), unlike WHERE which filters individual rows before grouping.

practice.question: A LEFT OUTER JOIN between tables A and B returns:

options.text: Only matching rows
All rows from A, with matching rows from B where available, and NULLs for B's columns when there is no match
Only rows from B
Only rows with no match in either table

practice.explanation: LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps every row from the left table, filling in NULLs for right-table columns whenever no matching row exists in the right table.

practice.question: A subquery used with the IN operator, such as "WHERE DeptID IN (SELECT DeptID FROM Department WHERE Location = 'NYC')", is an example of:

options.text: A correlated subquery
An uncorrelated (independent) subquery that can be evaluated once, separately from the outer query
A syntax error
A view

practice.explanation: This subquery does not reference any column from the outer query, so it can be evaluated independently and its result reused.

practice.question: Which relational algebra operator, symbolized by pi (π), extracts specific columns (attributes) from a relation?

options.text: Selection (σ)
Projection (π)
Set difference (−)
Cartesian product (×)

practice.explanation: Projection (π) produces a new relation containing only the specified attributes, dropping all others.

practice.question: What does the set difference operator R − S return?

options.text: Tuples that are in both R and S
Tuples that are in R but NOT in S
Tuples that are in S but not R
All tuples from R and S combined

practice.explanation: R − S returns exactly the tuples found in relation R that do not appear in relation S.

practice.question: The natural join operator (⋈) between two relations automatically:

options.text: Returns the Cartesian product with no filtering
Joins on attributes with the same name in both relations and removes the duplicate join column from the result
Requires explicitly specifying a join condition every time
Can only be used on relations with no shared attribute names

practice.explanation: A natural join implicitly equates attributes that share the same name in both relations and keeps only one copy of each such attribute in the output.

practice.question: A theta join (R ⋈θ S) differs from a natural join because:

options.text: It can use any comparison condition (θ), not just equality on same-named attributes, and does not automatically remove duplicate columns
It can only be performed on identical relations
It never removes any tuples
It is identical to a Cartesian product with no condition

practice.explanation: A theta join allows an arbitrary condition θ, and unlike a natural join it does not automatically eliminate duplicate attribute columns.

practice.question: The Division operator (R ÷ S) in relational algebra is typically used to answer queries phrased as:

options.text: "Find all tuples in R that match at least one tuple in S"
"Find values of R's attributes that are associated with ALL tuples/values in S" (a "for all" type query)
"Find the Cartesian product of R and S"
"Find tuples unique to R"

practice.explanation: Division answers "for all" style queries, such as finding students who have enrolled in EVERY course listed in another relation.

practice.question: In a functional dependency X → Y, X is referred to as the:

options.text: Dependent
Determinant (or left-hand side)
Foreign key
Candidate value

practice.explanation: X is called the determinant because its value determines the value of Y; X is also called the left-hand side (LHS) of the FD.

practice.question: If attribute set X functionally determines ALL other attributes of a relation, and no proper subset of X does, X is called a:

options.text: Foreign key
Candidate key
Derived attribute
Partial dependency

practice.explanation: A candidate key is a minimal attribute set that functionally determines every other attribute in the relation.

practice.question: The "transitivity" rule of Armstrong's axioms states that if X → Y and Y → Z both hold, then:

options.text: Z → X must also hold
X → Z holds
Y is a candidate key
X and Z are unrelated

practice.explanation: Transitivity allows chaining dependencies: if X determines Y, and Y determines Z, then X also determines Z.

practice.question: The "closure" of an attribute set X (denoted X+) with respect to a set of FDs F is defined as:

options.text: The set of all attributes that X can be derived from
The set of all attributes that are functionally determined by X, given F
The number of candidate keys in the relation
The set of attributes not related to X

practice.explanation: X+ is the set of every attribute that can be inferred to be functionally dependent on X using the given FDs and Armstrong's axioms.

practice.question: A "partial dependency" exists when:

options.text: A non-prime attribute depends on the whole of a composite candidate key
A non-prime attribute depends on only part (a proper subset) of a composite candidate key, not the whole key
Every attribute depends on every key
No dependency exists at all

practice.explanation: A partial dependency occurs when a non-prime attribute is functionally dependent on a proper subset of a composite key, rather than requiring the full key.

practice.question: A relation is in Second Normal Form (2NF) if it is in 1NF AND:

options.text: It has no composite candidate key at all
Every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole of every candidate key (no partial dependencies)
Every attribute is a foreign key
It has exactly two attributes

practice.explanation: 2NF additionally requires eliminating partial dependencies - cases where a non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key.

practice.question: A relation is in Third Normal Form (3NF) if it is in 2NF AND:

options.text: No non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key (i.e., no non-prime attribute depends on another non-prime attribute)
It has only one attribute
Every attribute is unique across all rows
It cannot have any foreign keys

practice.explanation: 3NF eliminates transitive dependencies: a non-prime attribute should not depend on another non-prime attribute, only directly on a candidate key.

practice.question: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) strengthens 3NF by requiring that for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y:

options.text: Y must be a prime attribute
X must be a superkey of the relation
Y must be a candidate key
X must contain at least two attributes

practice.explanation: BCNF requires that the determinant (left-hand side) of every non-trivial functional dependency be a superkey.

practice.question: Which anomaly specifically refers to the inability to insert a new fact into a database because an unrelated required attribute lacks a value yet?

options.text: Update anomaly
Insertion anomaly
Deletion anomaly
Selection anomaly

practice.explanation: An insertion anomaly occurs when inserting valid data about one entity is blocked because the table requires values for a different, not-yet-available entity.

practice.question: Given relation Employee(EmpID, DeptID, DeptLocation) where EmpID → DeptID and DeptID → DeptLocation, the dependency EmpID → DeptLocation is best described as a:

options.text: Partial dependency
Transitive dependency, since it is derived through the intermediate non-prime attribute DeptID
Trivial dependency
Multivalued dependency

practice.explanation: EmpID determines DeptLocation only indirectly, by way of DeptID (another non-prime attribute) - this chain is exactly what defines a transitive dependency.

practice.question: A relation can be in 3NF but NOT in BCNF when:

options.text: It has no candidate keys at all
There exists a functional dependency X → Y where X is NOT a superkey, but Y happens to be a prime attribute (part of some candidate key)
It has only one attribute
All its attributes are prime

practice.explanation: 3NF allows a dependency X → Y to exist even if X is not a superkey, as long as Y is a prime attribute - this exception is exactly what BCNF removes.

practice.question: Which ACID property ensures that a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state, satisfying all defined integrity constraints?

options.text: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability

practice.explanation: Consistency ensures that a transaction, upon completion, leaves the database in a state that satisfies all declared constraints and business rules.

practice.question: Which ACID property guarantees that once a transaction commits, its changes survive even a subsequent system crash or power failure?

options.text: Isolation
Durability
Atomicity
Consistency

practice.explanation: Durability ensures that committed changes are permanently recorded and will not be lost even if the system crashes immediately afterward.

practice.question: Which ACID property specifically ensures that the intermediate, uncommitted effects of one transaction are not visible to other concurrently executing transactions?

options.text: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability

practice.explanation: Isolation ensures that concurrently running transactions do not observe each other's intermediate, uncommitted state, as if each were executing alone.

practice.question: A "serial schedule" for a set of transactions is one where:

options.text: Operations of different transactions are arbitrarily interleaved
Transactions execute one at a time to completion, with no interleaving of operations between different transactions
All transactions run simultaneously with no ordering
Only read operations are allowed

practice.explanation: In a serial schedule, each transaction runs to completion before the next one starts.

practice.question: A schedule is called "serializable" if:

options.text: It must physically execute transactions one after another with no concurrency allowed
Its effect (final database state and output) is equivalent to that of some serial schedule of the same transactions
It always executes faster than a serial schedule
It contains no read operations

practice.explanation: A serializable schedule may interleave operations for better performance, but its overall effect must match some valid serial execution of the same transactions.

practice.question: An "exclusive lock" (X-lock) on a data item:

options.text: Can be held simultaneously by multiple transactions for reading
Allows only the single transaction holding it to read and write the item; no other transaction may hold any lock on it simultaneously
Is the same as a shared lock
Cannot be used for writing

practice.explanation: An exclusive lock grants the holding transaction sole read/write access, blocking all other transactions from acquiring any lock on that item.

practice.question: The Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol divides a transaction's locking actions into which two phases?

options.text: Read phase and write phase
Growing phase (acquiring locks) and shrinking phase (releasing locks)
Commit phase and abort phase
Lock phase and unlock phase, which can be interleaved freely

practice.explanation: In 2PL, a transaction first only acquires locks (growing phase), then, after its first release, only releases locks (shrinking phase).

practice.question: A "deadlock" in concurrency control occurs when:

options.text: A single transaction runs very slowly
Two or more transactions are each waiting for a resource (lock) held by another in the group, forming a cycle, so none can proceed
A transaction commits successfully
The database runs out of disk space

practice.explanation: Deadlock is a circular wait condition where each transaction in a cycle is blocked waiting for a lock held by another transaction in that same cycle.

practice.question: A "wait-for graph" used for deadlock detection represents:

options.text: The physical layout of database files
A directed graph where an edge from Ti to Tj means Ti is waiting for a lock held by Tj; a cycle in this graph indicates a deadlock
The order in which transactions were submitted
A list of all committed transactions

practice.explanation: In a wait-for graph, nodes are transactions, and a directed edge Ti → Tj means transaction Ti is blocked waiting on a resource held by Tj; a cycle indicates deadlock.

practice.question: In timestamp-based concurrency control, each transaction is assigned a unique timestamp primarily used to:

options.text: Determine the physical location of its data on disk
Decide the relative serialization order among concurrent transactions, ensuring consistency with that order
Set the transaction's priority for CPU scheduling
Encrypt the transaction's data

practice.explanation: Timestamps establish a fixed logical ordering among transactions; the protocol uses them to detect and reject operations that would violate this intended serialization order.

practice.question: A "clustered index" determines:

options.text: Nothing about physical storage; it is purely a logical concept
The physical order in which table rows are actually stored on disk
Only the order of index entries, never the table rows themselves
That the table must have no primary key

practice.explanation: A clustered index physically reorders (or stores) the table's rows according to the index key.

practice.question: A B+ tree index organizes data such that:

options.text: All actual data/key values are stored only in internal (non-leaf) nodes
All actual key values (often with row pointers) are stored in the leaf nodes, which are linked together, while internal nodes only guide the search
There is only one node in the whole structure
Leaf nodes are not connected to each other at all

practice.explanation: In a B+ tree, internal nodes contain only guide/separator keys for navigation, while all actual key values reside in the linked leaf level.

practice.question: A hash index is generally most efficient for which type of query?

options.text: Range queries like "find all values between 10 and 50"
Exact-match (equality) lookups like "find the row where key = 42"
Sorting the entire table
Finding the maximum value in a column

practice.explanation: A hash index computes a hash of the search key to directly locate the bucket containing matching rows, which is extremely fast for exact-match lookups but does not support efficient range queries.

practice.question: A "dense index" contains an index entry for:

options.text: Only the first record of each distinct block of data
Every single search key value (record) in the data file
Only even-numbered records
No records at all, just a pointer to the whole file

practice.explanation: A dense index has one index entry per record in the data file, in contrast to a sparse index.

practice.question: A "multilevel index" is used primarily to address the problem that:

options.text: A single-level index on a very large file can itself become too large to search efficiently (e.g., requiring many disk reads for binary search)
Databases cannot have more than one index per table
Indexes cannot be stored on disk
Hash indexes always outperform B+ trees

practice.explanation: When even the first-level index becomes large, a multilevel index builds an index-on-the-index so that searching reduces to a small number of fast steps.
